title: How To Develop Good Listening The First Month Of School nth-of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin frames poor listening among a new group of students as an expected, unremarkable problem rather than something to complain about, and shifts focus to what a teacher can control: how they speak. He offers a set of concrete speaking habits meant to build a listening habit—standing in one place, softening the voice, refusing to repeat instructions, cutting unnecessary words, pausing often, and focusing language on what students should do rather than what they shouldn't. Each habit is explained through its effect on attention: a softer voice requires active leaning-in, refusal to repeat forces first-time listening, and pausing gives students time to process while adding authority and drama. He closes by reframing the entire issue: poor listening isn't a student failing but a teacher's opportunity to change how they communicate.
points: Softening your voice, rather than talking louder, forces students into active rather than passive listening.
Refusing to repeat instructions removes the incentive for students to tune out the first time.
Cutting unnecessary words and pausing often makes instructions more memorable and gives students time to process.
Framing directions around what students should do, rather than what they shouldn't, engages their visualization and is inherently more interesting.
Poor classroom listening is fundamentally a teacher communication issue to solve, not a student deficiency to complain about.
quotes: Dwelling on it or complaining about it—as many teachers are wont to do—is a waste of time.
When it comes to developing good listening, the key is to speak in a way that will cause your students to tune in naturally.
Most teachers talk too loud, believing that it helps students pay attention. But the truth is, it does the opposite.
Repeating yourself effectively removes any reason for your students to listen to you the first time.
The fewer words you use, the better your students will listen.
Remembering to pause will give your students a moment to download the previous information.
But good listening isn’t about the students. It’s about the teacher.
